article_text:
Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey , starring Matt Damon, Anne Hathaway, Tom Holland, Robert Pattinson, Zendaya, and more, is undoubtedly one of the most anticipated films of the year. Last week, FC Contributing Editor Genevieve Yue wrote about Nolan’s latest, calling it a “strangely bloodless” adaptation of Homer’s epic poem. Genevieve writes: “ The film is shrouded in Nolan’s characteristic dourness, so that Homer’s lively world of men and gods is purged of lightness and humor. Odysseus’s homecoming brings relief, but not joy. A lot of people cry, but no one laughs except the suitors, whose sport is to insult beggars. Even the Sirens’ song, famed for its irresistibility, causes Odysseus to wail in grief.”

For this week’s Podcast, Film Comment Editor Clinton Krute invited Genevieve and fellow FC Contributing Editor Inney Prakash to discuss how the film fits within Nolan’s body of work, how it stacks up against other cinematic adaptations of The Odyssey , and more.

article_text:
‘D oes this whole Edward Cullen act actually work?” A distinct Twilight feeling is in the air in this initially enlivening vampire flick, with willowy twentysomething mortal Gemma (Nell Verlaque) caught in the middle of a pointy-toothed tug of war between tender Italian hunk Sebastian (Alvise Rigo) and her bad boy ex Eric (Kieron Moore). When she strolls with her friends into a hot vampire carnival, the ab count nearly outdoes the haemoglobin one. But this good-looking whirligig winds up disappointingly disjointed.

Gemma is still regrouping after her father’s suicide, an unspecified amount of time earlier. So her mum is relieved when she takes a night off from grieving by checking out the local fair with pals Ryan (Corrado Martini) and Olivia (Pauline Chávez). Absent for many years, creepy Eric has apparently joined the circus, featuring as the ostentatiously self-harming Man Who Feels No Pain. But when Sebastian invites Gemma into the carnival’s orgiastic inner sanctum, she learns they are a coven of bloodsuckers who, under leader Toussaint (Jason Isaac), have a strict no-killing code of conduct. Or, in the case of potential initiates like Gemma, obtaining consent. “No means no,” says immortal softboi Sebastian.

As befits any self-respecting ringmasters, directors David Charbonier and Justin Douglas Powell operate with much visual panache. They announce the trio’s entrance into the carnival with a splendid one-shot, tracking them, the denizens and local cop Dan (Cedrick Cooper). Later, they mount a crystalline confrontation between Ryan and Eric in a hall of mirrors. But, as with such stage endeavours, some of the effects are a bit cheesy: the supposedly Dionysian bolthole comes over more like a gastropub on deep-house DJ night. And Isaacs, playing the head vamp like a Rada fetish Gandalf, is at odds with the tone of what was previously a pleasingly downbeat slice of American alt.culturedom.

The emphasis on general flamboyant ambience is more detrimental story-wise. In particular, the film vacillates between positioning the increasingly insubordinate Eric as kooky undead loose cannon and genuine tragic antihero, though the charismatic Moore does a lot to tie him into a satisfying, lethal whole. The schism in vampire philosophies is underexplored, and not enough ground is laid for the final reveal about Gemma and Eric’s troubled backstories. To turn Sebastian’s come-on to Gemma on its head, Vampire Carnival is too taken with the illusion instead of the truth.

Attrice, socialite, amazzone, appassionata di giardinaggio. E anche una delle celebri “Swans” di Truman Capote . La figura di Lucy Douglas “C.Z.” Guest (1920-2003) è al centro di C.Z. Guest: Portrait of an American Style Icon , mostra aperta fino al 21 febbraio 2027 allo SCAD FASH Museum of Fashion + Film di Atlanta. Curata da Stefano Tonchi con Ariel Stark e realizzata con il sostegno di Max Mara , l’esposizione ricostruisce la sua biografia attraverso abiti, accessori, fotografie e materiali d’archivio.

Guest attraversò diversi ambienti della società americana del Novecento, passando da una breve esperienza nello spettacolo alla mondanità internazionale, fino a diventare una presenza ricorrente nelle cronache di costume e nelle fotografie di autori come Slim Aarons . Inserita nel 1959 nella International Best Dressed List Hall of Fame, fu inoltre musa di Salvador Dalí e Diego Rivera , mentre Capote la incluse nel gruppo delle donne dell’alta società americana che lo scrittore avrebbe reso celebri con la definizione di “Swans”, cigni.

Abiti da sera e tenute equestri

Per la prima volta la mostra riunisce un nucleo consistente della collezione personale di C.Z. Guest, oggi conservata allo SCAD Museum of Art grazie alla donazione della figlia Cornelia Guest , insieme ad alcuni prestiti provenienti dal Metropolitan Museum of Art di New York.

Sono esposti oltre 40 ensemble e accessori firmati da alcuni dei principali protagonisti della moda del Novecento, tra cui Mainbocher , Adolfo Sardiña , Oscar de la Renta , Valentino , Courrèges , Chanel , Carolina Herrera , Huntsman Savile Row e Max Mara.

Il percorso mette in relazione le diverse dimensioni della vita di Guest, tra formalità e vita all’aperto, mondanità e quotidianità. Accanto agli abiti da sera e ai completi indossati negli appuntamenti mondani compaiono capi da equitazione, sportswear e tenute destinate al giardinaggio nelle proprietà di Long Island e Palm Beach.

La stessa Cornelia Guest ha spiegato di aver affidato gli abiti della madre allo SCAD perché fossero utilizzati anche come materiali di studio, permettendo agli studenti di osservarne direttamente costruzione, tecniche e lavorazioni.

C.Z. Guest attraverso la fotografia

A mettere gli abiti in relazione con i luoghi e con la vita della protagonista contribuisce un ampio apparato fotografico. Le immagini provengono da archivi familiari e documentano Guest nel corso di diversi decenni, dagli anni di Hollywood alla vita sociale degli anni Cinquanta e Sessanta, fino agli eventi pubblici della maturità.

Particolarmente importante è il lavoro di Slim Aarons, fotografo che ha costruito attraverso le immagini della società internazionale del secondo dopoguerra un vero repertorio visivo di ville, resort, feste e rituali dell’alta società. Guest compare nelle sue fotografie tra gli Hamptons e Palm Beach, alternando occasioni pubbliche, vita privata e attività all’aperto. Il percorso comprende anche fotografie di Cecil Beaton , Irving Penn , Bruce Weber e Ron Galella .

Le Swans di Capote per l’alta società americana

Nata a Boston nel 1920 come Lucy Douglas Cochrane, C.Z. Guest proveniva da una famiglia appartenente all’élite cittadina. Dopo il debutto in società alla fine degli anni Trenta e una breve esperienza come showgirl e attrice, nel 1947 sposò Winston Frederick Churchill Guest , giocatore di polo e cugino di Winston Churchill.

Negli anni successivi divenne una delle figure più fotografate e riconoscibili dell’alta società americana. La combinazione tra abiti sartoriali, sportswear e capi equestri contribuì a definirne un’immagine distante dagli eccessi della mondanità più convenzionale, sintetizzata da Capote nell’espressione «cool vanilla lady».

La mostra segue quindi non solo una successione di firme e creazioni ma anche i contesti nei quali Guest costruì e mantenne la propria presenza pubblica: Hollywood, le relazioni mondane, l’equitazione, le proprietà di campagna e il circuito internazionale della moda.

Il rapporto con Max Mara

Tra i capi esposti figurano anche quattro creazioni di Max Mara. Il rapporto tra C.Z. Guest e la maison italiana risale almeno agli anni Novanta: nell’autunno-inverno 1995 Guest fu protagonista di un servizio per MM Magazine , anch’esso incluso nel percorso espositivo.

«Oltre al legame personale nato con C.Z. Guest in occasione dello shooting per MM Magazine nell’autunno/inverno 1995, servizio a sua volta incluso nel percorso espositivo, nel suo guardaroba sono presenti diversi capi Max Mara, quattro dei quali sono ora esposti», ha ricordato Giorgio Guidotti , Vice President Worldwide PR & Communications della maison.

La mostra coinvolge inoltre gli studenti dello SCAD di corsi che spaziano dalla moda alla fotografia, dal marketing alla gestione del lusso, fino al cinema e alla scrittura. In occasione dell’apertura è stato presentato anche un documentario prodotto dall’università sulla vita di Guest.

Source: A24 / Lionsgate

‘You Can See everything’, ‘the hunger games: sunrise on the reaping’

Lionsgate’s The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping is the biggest new release in UK and Ireland cinemas this weekend as A24’s You Can See Everything gets the widest ever opening for a non-music documentary.

Sunrise On The Reaping is out in 660 locations and is the widest opening for The Hunger Games films as well as Lionsgate’s second-widest opening of all time. The film made nearly £2m in previews on Wednesday (November 18).

It marks the sixth entry in The Hunger Games franchise, which is based on the young adult novels by Suzanne Collins. The highest-grossing was 2013’s Catching Fire with a £12.2m debut and £34.2m cume while the lowest-grossing was its most recent instalment, 2023’s The Ballad Of Songbirds And Snakes , which opened on £5.4m and finished at £18.2m.

Francis Lawrence returns to direct Sunrise On The Reaping , having directed all but one of the previous entries. The new film is set 24 years before the original trilogy and centres on the 50 th games. The cast is led by Mckenna Grace, Joseph Zada, Ralph Fiennes, Jesse Plemons, Elle Fanning, Glenn Close and Kieran Culkin with appearances from original stars Jennifer Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson.

A24’s eagerly anticipated Elizabeth Holmes documentary You Can See Everything finally launches in the UK in around 590 venues, with Holdover handling distribution on its behalf. This makes it the widest ever opening for a non-music documentary, ahead of Ocean With David Attenborough which debuted in 531 venues last year.

That title opened on £577,000 for a cume of £1.7m but the highest-grossing non-music documentary in the UK and Ireland is Michael Moore’s 2003 film Fahrenheit 9/11 which grossed £6.5m after opening on £1.3m.

Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s film will be hoping to at least match that thanks to an unprecedented level of word of mouth since opening in North America last month, where it has already grossed $90m. Many screenings over the weekend are already sold out, with venues continuing to be added, and excitement particularly strong among Gen Z and under-35s.

You Can See Everything follows Holmes, who was convicted of fraud over her health technology company Theranos, in the days leading up to her 11-year prison sentence. It first premiered at Telluride as a surprise screening before going on to New York Film Festival.

Helen Mirren, Your Mother and Sundance winner

In event cinema, Trafalgar Releasing has screenings of theatre production Giant , starring John Lithgow as Roald Dahl, in 462 locations and live concert BTS World Tour ‘Arirang’ In Kaohsiung in 200. Vue Lumiere has Cbeebies Panto 2026: Treasure Island in 381 locations.

Helen Mirren stars in A Talent For Murder which Universal is opening in 353 venues. Anton Corbijn’s film follows a junior literary editor who travels to Switzerland to try and persuade acclaimed novelist Patricia Highsmith to write another instalment of the Ripley books. Alden Ehrenreich and Olivia Cooke also star.

Source: Toronto Film Festival

‘Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother’

Amazon MGM has Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother in 215 cinemas. Mahershala Ali stars in Bassim Tariq’s thriller, which first premiered in Toronto, as a devoutly religious hitman and recent widower navigating grief, family and survival. Further cast include John Cho, Giancarlo Esposito and Tramell Tilmman.

Park Circus is re-releasing the 2011 animation Arthur Christmas in 151 locations.

Curzon is launching Sundance award-winner Josephine in 52 sites. Beth de Araujo’s film centres on an eight-year-old girl who witnesses a sexual assault. It won the grand jury prize and the audience award in Sundance before going on to screen at Berlinale and BFI London. Channing Tatum and Gemma Chan star.

Poh Si Teng’s war documentary American Doctor opens in 11 cinemas for Conic Film. The Sundance premiere follows three American doctors – Palestinian, Jewish and Zoroastrian – who travel to Gaza to provide medical aid.

BFI Distribution is releasing dark comedy Filipiñana in six venues. Rafael Manuel’s debut follows a 17-year-old girl working as a “tee-girl” at a posh golf resort in the Philippines. It won the special jury award for creative vision at Sundance and is also the country’s entry for best international feature at the Oscars.

Further releases include animated Cinderella reimagining Steps via Netflix; Belgian-set drama Heysel 85 via Icon Film Distribution; football documentary The Match via Disney; and Indian films Sathyavan Savithri and 70 Syaal via Zee Studios.

article_text:
Guitar Wolf , a real-life punk outfit with a long record of touring internationally, headlines “ Wild Zero Overdrive ,” director Takeuchi Tetsuro’s follow-up to his 1999 film “Wild Zero.”

The project is among those at this year’s Tokyo Gap-Financing Market .

Takeuchi said he is using the original as a template and updating it for the present day. “Precisely because we’re living in the age of AI, I want to convey the heat that comes from raw, primal punk rock,” Takeuchi said.

The Japan-Canada project is produced by Takegei Company Limited. Takeuchi is putting together the budget with his own money as the base, while also searching for distribution partners. Casting is underway.

“Rock’n’roll never dies. And love for Japanese subculture and rock’n’roll. UFOs. Motorcycles. Love,” Takeuchi said of what he wants audiences to take from the film.

“I’ve been a huge fan of ‘Wild Zero’ (1999) ever since it came out. I even named my dog Ace, after the film’s main character.” said Toronto-based producer Takabatake Aki.

Takabatake met the new film’s cinematographer by chance in Toronto, while Takabatake was working on a commercial, and took the encounter as a sign.

“‘Wild Zero Overdrive’ and I are bound together by an unbreakable rock ’n’ roll pact,” Takabatake said.

In Tokyo, the team will pitch the project to industry professionals at TGFM / Frontières Tokyo. The producers are also looking for further financing, distributors in Japan and abroad, and international sales agents.

“Hopefully, we’ll be able to connect with some great potential partners who share our passion for the project,” Takabatake said.

The Tokyo Gap-Financing Market runs as part of TIFFCOM, the content market attached to the Tokyo International Film Festival .

Guggenheim 2026: Allison Grant

© Allison Grant, left: Elvira Holding Saint Andrew’s Cross, right: Isa Holding Camphor Weed

Over the next few months, we are featuring the work of many of the 2026 Guggenheim Fellows as a way to celebrate their achievements and understand legacies and projects that have brought them this tremendous recognition.

The Board of Trustees of the John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation announced their appointment of the 101st class of Guggenheim Fellows, including 223 distinguished individuals working across 55 disciplines. Chosen through a rigorous application and peer review process from a pool of nearly 5,000 applicants, the Class of 2026 Guggenheim Fellows was tapped based on both prior career achievement and exceptional promise. As established in 1925 by founder Senator Simon Guggenheim, each Fellow receives a monetary stipend to pursue independent work at the highest level under “the freest possible conditions.”

“Our new class of Guggenheim Fellows is representative of the world’s best thinkers, innovators, and creators in art, science, and scholarship,” said Edward Hirsch, award-winning poet and President of the Guggenheim Foundation. “As the Foundation enters its second century and looks to the future, I feel confident that this new class of 223 individuals will do bold and inspiring work, undaunted by the challenges ahead. We are honored to support their visionary contributions.”

Allison Grant is an artist and Associate Professor of Photography at The University of Alabama.

Her artworks have been widely exhibited and are held in collections at institutions including the

Bainbridge Island Museum of Art, Birmingham Museum of Art, High Museum of Art, and the Museum of Contemporary Photography. Her work has been published in The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal. She is a 2026 Guggenheim Fellow and was named to the Silver Eye Center for Photography’s 2022 Silver List, among other honors. She lives and works in Tuscaloosa, Alabama.

Find her on Instagram @allie__grant

© Allison Grant, Installation and artist book in the exhibition We Handed Them to Others, As All Good Gardeners Do, Spring Grove Art Gallery at The University of Alabama, Huntsville, Installation Photo by Makalya Miller (4812 Photography)

I was moved when I saw work from your earlier project at the Dangerous Landscapes exhibit at Alabama Contemporary Art Center. Knowing the potential impact of your work during this particular time in history, I was excited to read that you had been awarded a Guggenheim Fellowship and were working on a new project. What does receiving a fellowship mean to you at this stage of your career?

Thanks Karen, I remember talking with you about Dangerous Landscapes . That exhibit was one of the first times I experimented with an installation that invites audience participation. My new work that was awarded a Guggenheim builds on that interest.

But to answer your question, winning a Guggenheim has given me a year to dedicate myself to my art practice full time, which is an incredible gift. In addition to being an artist, I’m also an educator, parent, and sometimes I curate. I love it all, but it’s a lot to manage. As my career has expanded, each of these parts of my life has required more and more attention, and I am always scraping together time and trying to invest further. It can be especially challenging because I make long-term bodies of work that are deeply researched and require a lot of focused consideration. I feel unbelievably fortunate to receive the funds and support to dedicate myself to making new work, and I’m so excited to see what this opportunity makes possible.

© Allison Grant, Top: Lorelei Holding Beebalm, bottom: Kelly and Gwen Holding Tansy

© Allison Grant, Top: Lorelei Holding Beebalm, bottom: Kelly and Gwen Holding Tansy

Did the fellowship validate something you already knew about your work, or did it change how you see your practice?

I have spent the last ten years living and working in Tuscaloosa, Alabama. It is a place with a lot of political and social tension, but also one that is often stereotyped and flattened by the national news media and ignored by the contemporary art world. In my work and life, I’ve become interested in broadening the ways the Deep South is seen and known in relation to national and international issues, and forging possibilities for coalitions and understanding with people from other regions. The Guggenheim is a kind of affirmation of the work I’ve done in community, and to me it also draws attention to a place and its people, and not just me as an artist. What the fellowship validated for me is the power of working alongside others through a practice that is braided with the wisdom, strength, and openness of my community, and especially people I’ve come to know in the American South.

The award felt extra gratifying because Jeremiah Ariaz and Harlan Bozeman , who both live in the Deep South, and Chris Aluka Berry , who works in Appalachia, were in the same cohort as me. Seeing them awarded felt like a further recognition that the stories coming out of overlooked regions of America are finding a larger place in contemporary art.

© Allison Grant, Seif Holding Hellebore

Tell us about your current project.

It’s called Holding Together . For the past two years, I’ve been photographing people in Alabama and other parts of the US while they hold plants that have been historically used for contraception, abortion, or infertility treatment.

The 2022 Dobbs decision made reproductive healthcare much more difficult to access, especially in the Deep South. I wanted to make a community portrait of people contending with this new legal landscape. I started researching plants that people used to try to manage fertility before modern medical treatments were available. Many of the plants have interesting histories: tansy and hellebore were documented as abortifacients in medieval monastic medical records [1] ; dogfennel is listed in the Native American Ethnobotany Database as an Indigenous abortifacient [1] ; cotton was used by enslaved Black women to induce abortion using knowledge brought from parts of Africa where cotton grows wild [2] ; and Queen Anne’s Lace has been used in various cultural contexts as an emergency contraceptive, including in Appalachian communities where people have sometimes been cut off from healthcare, physically and financially. [3]

Other folk remedies exist, too, but they are almost all ineffective or toxic, and should not be used. I wanted to work with my community to honor the long history of people using these plants, while also refusing to accept a world where they become someone’s only option today. As I photographed, subjects often shared stories of their experiences with reproductive healthcare and their motivations for participating. I started recording these stories and including transcriptions of them in installations as a way of embedding the present into longer histories.

When we were talking earlier about my exhibition at Alabama Contemporary, I mentioned my interest in involving visitors as participants. A few months ago, I showed two images from Holding Together at the Sarah Moody Art Gallery at The University of Alabama. Beneath the photographs were postcards with the same images that visitors could take and mail. Mail order abortion pills have been a critical lifeline for many people in states with bans, and the postcards are a way for viewers to participate in the project by symbolically mailing abortifacients. It’s one way I’m thinking about how I might extend this work beyond the gallery.

[1] John M. Riddle, Eve’s Herbs: A History of Contraception and Abortion in the West (Harvard University Press, 1997).

[1] Daniel E. Moerman, “Dogfennel,” Native American Ethnobotany, University of Michigan, Dearborn, accessed September 3, 2026, http://naeb.brit.org/uses/9140/.

[2] Dorothy Roberts, Killing the Black Body: Race, Reproduction, and the Meaning of Liberty (Pantheon Books, 1997).

[3] Gabrielle Claire Jansen and Hans Wohlmuth, “Carrot Seed for Contraception: A Review,” Australian Journal of Herbal Medicine 26, no. 1 (2014): 10–17.

© Allison Grant, T. and Maziyar Holding Rue

You mentioned your hope to forge possibilities for coalitions and understanding. Would you elaborate?

Yes, let me share a story that will help explain.

When the Dobbs decision was announced, I was visiting Chicago and while I was in town I attended a Women in the Arts luncheon. Many people at the event were processing the upsetting news we’d all heard that morning. I went to graduate school in Chicago, and I had a conversation with a few people from that community whom I deeply respect. They were angry because they believed that Southerners were to blame for a ruling that had made women and people with uteruses in Chicago unsafe.

In my opinion, that is a skewed understanding. There are people in the Deep South who fight for reproductive justice and work under some of the most difficult circumstances in the country. Their work is often unseen in other regions where people sometimes have a limited understanding of what is happening here. One motivation for this project is to push against bias against this region because it is not accurate. 48% of Alabamians believe abortion should be legal in most or all cases. [1]

I want to make art that brings visibility and support to the many people living in the Deep South who are fighting for the same things as the women I was talking with in Chicago on that day. I don’t share this story to humiliate or scold anyone. I want to work together, and one hope I have is that visibility will make space for coalitions and shared advocacy that is sometimes hindered by stereotypes about the South.

[1] Public Religion Research Institute, “Mapping Abortion Views Across the 50 States: Insights from PRRI’s2025 American Values Atlas,” April 23, 2026, https://prri.org/research/mapping-abortion-views-across-the-50-states-insights-from-prris-2025-american-values-atlas/ .

© Allison Grant, Installation and artist book in the exhibition We Handed Them to Others, As All Good Gardeners Do, Spring Grove Art Gallery at The University of Alabama, Huntsville, Installation Photo by Makalya Miller (4812 Photography)

How will you use the freedom The Guggenheim Fellowship provides?

I am working to expand the geographic reach and scope of Holding Together . Most of the photographs and interviews in the project have come from a network of contacts and reproductive healthcare advocacy organizations in Alabama. I want to incorporate a more robust understanding of how reproductive experiences differ across places, and I want that expansion to grow out of meaningful relationships that I build with people I meet and interact with in person. The fellowship will allow me to travel and follow what develops.

As I travel, I’d like to visit libraries and archives with collections that hold books, zines, and other parts of the material history of the transmission of reproductive medical knowledge. I’ve photographed older women who’ve described zines that circulated pre-internet with instructions on using herbal contraceptives and abortifacients. I’ve also found examples housed in academic libraries alongside books and archival materials that describe historic methods and experiences. Before contemporary pharmaceutical systems, botanical illustrations, and eventually photographic technologies, were essential tools for identifying plants and communicating knowledge about their medicinal uses.

These materials already play a role in my thinking. My photographs are printed on matte paper and they kind of look like a drawing. This is intentional—I am trying to nod to the history of botanical illustration and blur the line between drawing and photography, and between two-dimensional representation and photographic depth. As I continue to explore, I’m curious to see if more elements of research might inform or even enter my work.

I am also using this time to create a book. I think this project is perfectly suited to the intimacy and slowness a book can offer, and I’m excited by the drafts I’ve put together so far.

© Allison Grant, Bet Holding Hellebore

Thank you for sharing some of the pages from your upcoming book with us today. Your last book, Within The Bittersweet , was about raising your children amid concerns of climate change and pollution. It is a gorgeous book that merges themes of beauty and grief. Are there commonalities between that project and Holding Together?

Yes, many. Both projects are rooted in questions about how we care for ourselves and others while contending with difficult realities of our time.

They are also both filled with grief and awe at the many things women have survived. I don’t think people talk about the constant grief and complexity inside of pregnancy, motherhood or living in a body capable of reproduction nearly as much as it’s felt. I feel it is powerful to put that on display. Having public facing art exhibitions is very important to me because it creates a way for others to consider stories usually kept in private life.

© Allison Grant, Allison Holding Hellebore

© Allison Grant, SJW Holding Leatherleaf Mahonia, Constantine Holding Epazote and Wormwood

How has Holding Together impacted you as a mother, a woman, an educator, and an artist?

People have died in my community while waiting for an emergency D&C that doctors can’t give. Both this project and Within the Bittersweet have forced me to contend with the limits of my ability to protect myself and the people I love. I feel like every story I’ve recorded for Holding Together could have been me if I were born into different circumstances or with different anatomy, and I worry my daughters could live versions of those stories too. We are so lucky to live in a time when medical advances make high-quality care possible, but if we do not have access, our children and communities will not be safe. How does one show up in a world where that is true? Things will never change for the better if no one is willing to look it in the face, so that’s what I try to do with as much kindness and humility as I can.

© Allison Grant, Sydney Holding Cotton

© Allison Grant, Hallie Holding Queen Anne’s Lace, Sarah and Milo Holding Queen Anne’s Lace

As I read the words accompanying your photographs, I hear both vulnerability and courage in the sharing of these stories. Will you tell us a bit about creating an atmosphere of trust while working on this project? Also, have any of the people you have photographed and interviewed shared the impact of their participation in this project on their own lives?

Yes. It is important to me to avoid harming participants or anyone who is discussed in a story. I have interviewed immigrants and people who could face legal consequences, workplace backlash, or community ostracization for talking openly about these issues. Before I interview someone, I let them know that I won’t share their identity. After we finish, I transcribe what was said, clean it up, and take anything too specific out in consultation with the subject. Once they’ve signed off, I let them know where I’ll be publishing it and I tell them they can withdraw from the project at any time. I came up with this process with help from several community historians at The University of Alabama.

The photographs are titled with the first names of the subjects unless they ask me to withhold their identity. Names can signal background, identity, and ethnicity, and the pictures aren’t as specific, so my approach is a little different there.

A lot of the people I’ve included in my work find the process of participating cathartic. Reproductive healthcare has a profound impact on people’s lives. Sharing helps the narrator and the reader know they are not alone. Every time I photograph or interview someone, I feel a million times closer to them when we finish, and I think that’s mutual. It’s the best part of making the work.

Many of the stories I’m told end with a sense of healing or personal resolution. In difficult experiences, I think individuals need that kind of closure. But for the project, I often ask subjects if I can take those end parts out. On a societal level, their experiences echo things that are still happening. I think taking the resolution out makes the stories feel more true to the larger ideas in the project, and subjects usually agree.

© Allison Grant, Grace Holding Tansy

© Allison Grant, top: Grace Holding Tansy, bottom: Arielle Holding Juniper What has sustained your practice over the years?

Friendships and community, first and foremost. There are people who have been the first eyes and ears on my work for most of my adult life. I’ve found a kind of mutual trust in these relationships, and we’ve come to see each other’s perspectives in ways that are very deep and powerful.

Grants have also sustained my practice. The generous donors and organizations who offer financial support, like the Guggenheim, are a lifeline. We’ve been watching the federal government gut funding, and there is an implicit pressure that many institutions are weighing when they consider showing politically charged artwork. I’ve been really lucky to work with several organizations and institutions that are willing to hold space for viewpoints that are under attack. Not every museum or institution will do it, and it’s empowering to watch an organization put their values on the line alongside an artist instead of shrinking back.

© Allison Grant, Shakiba Holding Yarrow, Claire Holding Queen Anne’s Lace

© Allison Grant, Alesha Holding Queen Anne’s Lace

Thank you, Allison. In closing, what advice would you give to photographers for going through the process of applying for a fellowship?

Find a community and engage generously. Art is built through reciprocity and shared support, and your application will be stronger if you are submitting something that’s received feedback from people you trust.

I also think it’s important to consider what you have to gain if you don’t win. I applied three times. I learned so much about myself and my work every time. I had support readers who told me how strong my applications were and made me feel like I was moving my practice forward, even when I wasn’t awarded. That’s the way I try to look at all of the work that I do. Applying can affirm a belief in the value of my work that doesn’t have to be shredded every time I get a rejection.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Following the global success of F1, Apple and Damson Idris have found their next high-profile project on which to team. Sources tell Deadline that Apple Original Films is coming on to develop Sacrament , a new feature with Jonathan Levine attached to direct and Idris attached to produce.

Insiders add that film remains in early development, though the plan is to develop the film as a starring vehicle for Idris, the F1 star. The project will hail from Apple Studios , and Chernin Entertainment will produce via its first-look feature deal with Apple.

Written by Enzo Mileti & Scott Wilson, the film follows two Chicago cops-turned-contractors who track a runaway thief to a remote and fortified township in Sacrament, UT. What begins as a routine job escalates into a battle where they are outnumbered, outgunned and forced to become better partners.

Watch on Deadline

'The Gentlemen' Star Chanel Cresswell Boards Netflix's 'The Lords' Day'

Peter Chernin and David Ready will produce for Chernin Entertainment. Idris will produce under his Keep Quiet Productions banner, and Levine will produce alongside Gillian Bohrer through their company MegaMix.

Following the success of F1: The Movie, which grossed $634 million worldwide and scored multiple Oscar nominations including Best Picture, Idris and Apple were looking to partner again. It was Chernin that approached Idris with the script. The project also reunites Idris with Mileti and Wilson, who worked with him on his hit FX series Snowfall.

Idris is currently filming the the Miles Davis pic Miles & Juliette from director Bill Pohlad and also has the Netflix series The Lords’ Day, which he also executive produced.

As for Levine, the director has become sought after with buzz growing on his upcoming sports drama Mr. Irrelevant, which bows on Christmas Day. That buzz was so loud that Tom Cruise asked to see the film; he was so impressed he tapped Levine to helm his sequel to the hit Paramount sports pic Days of Thunder .

Sacrament marks the latest feature development for Apple and Chernin Entertainment, joining titles including One Month Mark, Last Flight Out and Five Secrets . Chernin Entertainment has also produced multiple projects for Apple TV including the epic Chief of War and the Emmy-nominated See both with Jason Momoa, Truth Be Told starring Octavia Spencer and Gabrielle Union, and Emmy-winning documentary series The War for Football.

Besides Snowfall, Mileti and Wilson were also co-exec producers on the FX series Fargo. They are repped by WME, Untitled and lawyer Tara Kole at JSSK

Idris is repped by CAA, M88 and attorney John Meigs. Levine is repped by Goodman, Genow, Schenkman, Smelkinson & Christopher.

あなたが母親の手料理を食べられる回数は、あとどれくらい残ってますか？

劇場公開日： 2026年11月20日

解説・あらすじ

「パラサイト 半地下の家族」のチェ・ウシクとチャン・ヘジンが親子役で再共演し、“母親の手料理を食べられる回数”が見えるようになった息子と、何も知らずに息子を想う母親の姿を描いたファンタジードラマ。韓国で翻訳出版された上野そらによる小説「あなたが母親の手料理を食べられる回数は、残り328回です。」を原作に、キム・テヨン監督が故郷・釜山を舞台に自身の経験を交えながら描き出す。 釜山で母ウンシルと暮らすハミンは、ある日突然、目の前に謎の数字が現れるようになる。それは、母の手料理を食べるたびに減っていく“母の命のカウントダウン”だった。自分が母の手料理を食べなければ母を守れると考えたハミンは、さまざまな口実をつけて母の手料理を避けはじめる。やがて故郷を離れソウルでひとり暮らしをするハミンは、結婚を考えている恋人リョウンに、自分だけに見える数字の秘密を打ち明けるが……。 ハミンの恋人リョウン役に、「ハンサム・ガイズ」「おひとりさま族」などのコン・スンヨン。

article_text:
韓国・光州で、9月5日から11月15日まで開催されている 「第16回光州ビエンナーレ」 。シンガポールを拠点に活動するアーティストのホー・ツーニェンがアーティスティックディレクターを務める本展で、日本のキュレーターたちによる 「アサクサ館（パビリオン）」 が展開された。

東京・西浅草にあるプロジェクトスペース「アサクサ」のポップアップ形式としてこのプロジェクトを率いたのは、アサクサ代表で現在シンガポールを拠点とする 大坂紘一郎 、2017年からアサクサに参加し、東京とデュッセルドルフを拠点に活動する 三上真理子 、ウィーンとベルリンを拠点とする 根来美和 、ウィーンと松本および東京を拠点とする 丸山美佳 の4名。

2018年からナショナルパビリオン制を導入した光州ビエンナーレでパビリオンを展開するにあたり、かれらの共通の出発点にあったのは、「ナショナル」の枠組みを疑うことだった。「日本館」ではないかたちで、光州という民主化運動の歴史のある土地で何ができるのか。そうした問いに向き合いながら、光州の歴史文化地区にある楊林文化センターにアサクサ館展示「The Step After the Last Step」を作り上げた（参加作家：ハイドルン・ホルツファイント、菊地智子、小宮りさ麻吏奈、イ・ジュヨン、嶋田美子）。

ここでは、前回の「第15回光州ビエンナーレ」で初めて設置された日本パビリオンのキュレーションを手がけた 山本浩貴 を聞き手に迎え、アサクサ館プロジェクトチームの4人による座談会を行った。前編では、アサクサ館の成り立ちを振り返りながら、本展の軸となった「移動」「越境性」というテーマや個人の物語に光を当てること、そして光州での実践から見えてきたこれからのキュレーションのかたちを探る。後編では、「ナショナル」という概念そのものに立ち返り、キュラトリアル・ステートメントにおける言語化の問題、さらにはファンディングのあり方にまで議論を広げた。

アサクサ館設立のきっかけ

山本 まず、「アサクサ館」がスタートしたきっかけを教えてください。

根来 昨年、私が韓国のMMCA（国立現代美術館）でレジデンスをしていたとき、光州ビエンナーレ財団の方とお話しする機会があり、日本館のキュレーションをしないかと率直なオファーがありました。このテーマはのちほど話題に出ると思いますが、私としては、「ナショナル・パビリオン」という枠組みのなかで、しかも「光州」という場所で日本館のキュレーションをすることには戸惑いがありました。日本を「代表」する展覧会を企画することに戸惑いがあったからです。そこで、よく協働している丸山さんに相談して、東アジアの地政学的問題を批判的に扱ってきたスペース「アサクサ」を現在運営している大坂さん、三上さんにお話をもちかけました。

山本 根来さん、丸山さんからの声かけに、大坂さん、三上さんが応えるかたちで始まったと。

三上 そうなのですが、実際は単純な道のりではありませんでした。光州ビエンナーレのパビリオンに応募するには個人ではなくて団体である必要があり、山本さんがキュレーションされたとき（2024年）であれば、福岡市がバックアップに入っていたわけですよね。しかし、アサクサはインディペンデントの集いというのが実態に近く、団体として潤沢なリソースがあるわけでもなく、いつもプロジェクトごとにチームを組んで、資金を集めて運営してきました。なので、参加についてはずいぶんと悩みましたし、何度も大坂さんと話し合いました。

いっぽう、私はアサクサで国外作家を日本に招聘して東京でリサーチし、制作し、発表するプロジェクトに携わり、制作した作品数も増えてきたので、日本以外の場所でもアサクサで制作した作品を見せられないかとずっと考えており、「ポップアップ」の可能性について大坂さんとも度々話していました。そのようなこともあり、今回、光州でアサクサそのものをポップアップ的に見せる試みは、良いきっかけになるのではないかと思いました。ただ、ナショナル・パビリオン制というヴェネチア・ビエンナーレから始まった枠組みを光州が踏襲していることについて、枠組み自体や背景にある前提を疑っていくことは、当初からみんなに共有した問題意識としてありました。

山本 そうした問題意識のもと、みなさんのあいだで、具体的にどのような対話がなされたのですか。

丸山 「国を代表する」といった枠組みへの疑いというものは、私たち全員が最初から共有していたものでしたが、パビリオン制が国家という枠組みを前提にした制度である以上、こちら側がどれほどそれを避けようとしても、その枠組みを扱わざるをえない状況が出てくるだろうということはそれぞれが自覚していたと思います。だから、その枠組み自体を批判的に眺めることは果たしてできるのか、そして、アサクサというスペースは東京にありますが、私たち4人全員が日本出身のキュレーターで、現在は日本に住んでおらず、また大きなインスティテューションにも所属していないインディペンデントな立場から活動しているという観点からも考える必要もありました。

なので、日本というナショナルな枠組みに批判的な仕方で、「日本館」をやらずに何らかのかたちにすることはいかにして可能なのかを何度も話し合いました。そのとき、アーティストや展覧会ありきで話を進めるのではなく、まずは私たちが日本の歴史や文脈を背負いながらも、日本を拠点としておらず、しかし国境を越えたかたちでそれぞれが帝国主義や植民地主義に関連する調査や活動をしてきているということが反映されるような企画にしたいという想いがありました。

「光州」という場で起こる二重の問い

山本 「光州」という場を考慮すると、光州ビエンナーレで日本館をキュレーションする人が背負わざるをえない課題は二重性を抱えているように思います。つまり、ナショナルという枠組みを批判的に解体しつつ、いっぽうで日本の東アジアにおける帝国主義の歴史に由来するポジショナリティを引き受けなくてはならない。そうした二重性について、みなさんはどのように考えているのでしょうか。

根来 光州で展覧会を開催するうえで、帝国主義の歴史、その歴史が現在にもたらす影響、具体的には地政学的・政治的な関係性について、避けて通ることはできないと思います。近代に作られてきた暴力的な構造がいまも残っていて、それが亀裂や分断として現代世界に現れている。日本の文脈を背負っている者として、そこから語らなくてはいけないこともありますが、同時に、排他的なナショナリズムがますます強化され、軍産化が進み、環境危機が悪化し、紛争が頻発するといったような、現在私たちが生きているなかで目の当たりにする暴力的な構造をどう考えるべきか。こうした構造に対して、私たちは光州という場所でどのような対話ができるだろうか、どのような抵抗のかたちを思い描くことができるのか、そうした構造が覆い隠す周縁化された声をどう拾い集めることができるのかといったことを考えました。ですので、私としては、先ほど山本さんがおっしゃったような「二重性」を、自分たちが抱えなくてはいけない複雑性のひとつの軸としてとらえ直したいと考えています。

三上 そもそも、光州で「展覧会」という従来のフォーマットを実施すべきなのか、という点も話し合いました。キュレーターが4人集まっているわけなので、話し合いのプロセスや未完のものを敢えて提示し、そこから未来に開かれていくような何らかの「場」を創出できないか、資金に限りがあるので、いっそのこと「出版」のみするというアイデアもありました。そうした話し合いのなかで全員が共通して関心をもっていたのが「移動」や「越境性」というテーマでした。なかでも「移動」や「越境」のなかで生きた、あるいは生きている個人や存在の物語に光を当てたいと思いました。

参加アーティストの小宮りさ麻吏奈さんのマンガ『線場のひと』に出てくるセリフで「私たちは不自由な中でも選択はしている／それが選択させられているだけだとしても」というのが印象に残っています。流されているようにみえても、人はギリギリのところで何らかの選択をしていて、それはその人なりの抵抗の表現だったりもする。だから、今回の展示では、大きな主語ではなく、小さな主語としての個人がどのように移動したり、ある構造のなかで動いたりしているかに目を向けたいと思っていました。光州でのパビリオン・プロジェクトでしたので、日韓という枠も意識しながらも、オーストリアのハイドルン・ホルツファイントさんと制作した映像作品を含めました。これは、現在無期懲役で収監されている日本のある活動家からの手紙の朗読を通して、1960年代から現在まで続く日本各地の抵抗運動と都市風景を交差させる試みでした。

山本 大坂さんはいかがですか。アサクサでは満州をテーマに映像を制作したロイス・アンなど、東アジアの戦争と植民地主義の歴史、日本の帝国主義を扱った、ギャラリーや美術館では展示の難しい作品を紹介してきました。光州ビエンナーレでのパビリオンの話があったとき、どう思われましたか。

大坂 ビエンナーレやパビリオンという形式は、このメンバー、この機会でなければ、ぼくの選択肢にはないものでした。最近では、大きな会場で、大きなテーマを掲げて展覧会をすることが現実性を失ってきているようにも感じます。それは「展覧会」という過度に制度化されたフォーマット自体への疑いも含めてです。

それとぼくは（かつて日本が占領した）シンガポールを拠点にしてもう2年ほど経つのですが、行く先々で日本が戦時中に行ったことを目にしますし、日本の歴史的加害者性は当然認識されるべきものです。しかし、侵略した側がそれを認める・認めないにかかわらず、独立後の現実を現に乗り越えてきた多くの国にしてみれば、加害性を認めるだけでラディカルな表現とするような北半球のモラルも遅きに失した感があります。その先に何が描けるかという課題はつねに念頭にありました。なので、今回はそれぞれ考えの違いがあっても前提の問題を共有できるこのメンバーだからこそやりたいと思えました。

アーティストやキュレーターのあいだに生まれた一時的な共同体

山本 そうした話し合いを受けて、具体的にどのようにアーティストやコンセプトを決定していったのでしょうか。

丸山 国という大きな枠組みを批判的にとらえることを前提としながらも、小さな、日常の声を紡いでいくなかで、それがどのように大きな問題へとつながっていくか、あるいはつながらないかをキュレーションを通して考えることのほうが自分たちのやってきた実践に合っていると思いました。そう考えたとき、先にテーマを決めて、それに合わせてアーティストを呼ぶのは、どのくらい助成金がもらえるかどうかわからないこともあり、現実的ではないと思いました。

また、大きなテーマから入って、トップダウンの方向で決めていくことへの抵抗感もそれぞれが持っていたと思います。なので、まずは4人の興味や関心をシェアするところから始めて、根来さんも私も昨年に韓国に滞在していたこともあり、そこで出会った人や作品、話した内容を紹介し合うセッションなどを重ねました。そんななかで、「連想」のようなかたちで、少しずつ参加アーティストが決まっていきました。私はそのようにとらえているのですが、みなさんはどうですか。

根来 その通りだと思います。ラウンドテーブルのようなかたちで、それぞれの興味や自分がよりどころにしている思想、朝鮮半島や日本含め東アジアが抱える歴史や状況、あるいは韓国で出会ったアーティストについて共有していくことで、多種多様な素材が少しずつ集まっていった気がします。たんに結果としての展覧会作りだけではない、複数の知のあり方を模索するキュラトリアルなプラットフォームといった感じでしょうか。そうした複数の知がひとつにまとめられることなく並存しているというか。

そのなかで、菊地智子さん、イ・ジュヨンさん、小宮りさ麻里奈さん、そして嶋田美子さんの活動やリサーチがホルツファイントさんのリサーチへと有機的につながっていきました。キュレーター4人の共通認識として、単一の直線的なナラティブを紡ぐのではなく、それぞれの差異が消去されることなく存在したままゆるやかに関係し合っていくようなプロセスを志向していたというのはあったと思います。

三上 連想的につながっていたというのはその通りですが、キュレーターやアーティスト同士が、過去にそれぞれ別の場所で既に出会っており、互いに認識していたことも、不確定要素が大きかった今回のプロジェクトの中では、重要だったと思います。今回の参加者たちは、それぞれがもつ「磁場」が近いのかもしれません。「これほど参加作家が仲良くなった現場は初めて」という声も複数のアーティストからもらいました。韓国滞在中に一緒に登山したり、別の芸術祭を訪問したり、楽しんでいる様子がわかり、頼もしく、また微笑ましかったです。

根来 毎日、ランチもディナーも一緒なのが当たり前みたいな感じでした。程良いキンシップというか、何か不思議な関係性ができていたと思います。

三上 そう、アーティストとキュレーターだけでなく、地元のアーティストやアートワーカーたちを巻き込んだテンポラリーな共同体のようなものができあがっていたと感じています。

丸山 今回は潤沢なリソースがあったわけではないので、地元のアーティストやそのコミュニティの人たちの、精神的なものも含めたサポートなしでは成り立たなかったと思います。また、参加アーティストたちが光州で展示をすることで、そこから次の展開につながるような関係性ができるようにしたいというのは最初から意識していました。キャリア的な「ステップアップ」という意味ではなく、いい出会いやつながりを提供する場になればいいなというのは、みんなが考えていたことでした。

また、完成したものだけでなく、リサーチや制作のプロセスそのものをシェアしていくことは、私たちの関心であったという気がしています。それと「国家」のことに付け加えるとすれば、やはり今回の台湾館をめぐる出来事（＊）は重要な問いを突き付けているように思います。台湾館のキュレーターやほかのパビリオンのキュレーターが財団側に「台湾館」という名称を使用できるように要請し、そうした動きのなかで地元のアクティビストたちとのつながりも出来たので、そこから学んだこともとても多かったです。そういった人たちがアサクサ館の展示を観に来てくれて、そこでさらに会話が交わされる。そういったところから新しい何かが始まっていく感覚があります。

根来 それと、光州ビエンナーレはアジアのなかでも重要なビエンナーレとされていて、国際的な評価も高い。アーティスティック・ディレクターや参加作家も国際的に評価されている人たちが選ばれている。ですが、光州ビエンナーレが始まった重要な文脈として民主化運動と光州事件の歴史があり、地元の人たちが「光州スピリット」と呼んで大切にしている抵抗の精神があります。光州ビエンナーレはそうした精神を継承しながら、「アートに何ができるか」を提示していくというミッションを背負っているはずであった。ところが、実状は自由に移動のできるインターナショナルなアート関係者が社交する場になっていて、地元との交わりが希薄である気がします。

その意味で、地元のアクティビストや、独立系の書店を営む人、レジデンシーを運営する大学教授などの文化系の人たちと交流することができたことは貴重な経験でした。

＊──第16回光州ビエンナーレでは、国立台湾美術館が企画した展示の名称を、主催者側が当初の「Taiwan Pavilion(台湾館)」から美術館の略称による「NTMoFA館」に変更したとして、キュレーターや参加作家らが抗議した。その後ビエンナーレ側は「台湾館」の名称を認めたが、これに反発した中国館は開幕2日前に展示から撤退した。

キュレーションの新しいかたち

山本 そうした新しいキュレーションのかたちは新鮮に感じました。みなさんはそれぞれにキュレーターであり、リサーチャーでもありますが、これからキュレーションのかたちはどうなっていくと思いますか。新しいかたちのキュレーションが生まれてくるにともなって、キュレーターのあり方や役割は変わってくるのでしょうか。

三上 「インディペンデント」という状態は、キュレーションのあり方自体を疑える視点を持ちやすいと思います。インスティテューションのバックアップがない状態で場作りを仕掛けていくのはアクティビストにも近い動きかもしれない。私たちはキュレーターでもあるけれども、同時に交渉人でもあり、ときにフィクサー的な役割をしたり、プロデューサーでもトランスレーターでもあったりします。そうした様々な役割があって、場に応じてカメレオンのように動くといいますか。

活動場所が都度変わるプロジェクトでは、その場所の人たちとどのような関係性を結べるかが大事になってきます。現地の人にとって、私たちはやっぱり「他者」。遠くから来た客であり、新しい友人になれるかもしれない存在。そう考えると、テンポラリーなコミュニティ作りも、キュレーターの重要な役割のひとつではないかと思います。いっぽう、「メンテナンス」の重要性も痛感しました。資金や基盤が不安定なプロジェクトベースのチームが、こうした仕事を継続して担うことは簡単ではありませんでした。その意味で、インスティテューションに所属するハウス・キュレーターとインディペンデント・キュレーターとでは、担える役割や費やせるリソースは自ずと違ってくると、改めて思いました。

山本 ぼくが今回の光州ビエンナーレで感じたのは、アーティスティック・ディレクターの変化がキュレーションをめぐる変化に対応しているということでした。ニコラ・ブリオーのような「才気煥発」型の、大きな枠組みをつくるのが得意なキュレーターから、アーティストであるホー・ツーニェンのように有機的でローカルなコミュニティやネットワークを作っていくのが得意な人物へのシフト。同じことはカトリーヌ・ダヴィッドやオクウィ・エンヴェゾーがアーティスティック・ディレクターを務めたドクメンタがルアンルパを起用したことにも表れている。

新奇性のある大きな枠組みを提示して、そこにアーティストを配置していくかたちの（ユニークな個が主導する）キュレーションから、それぞれのリソースを共有しながらオーガニックなつながりを作っていくかたちの（しばしばチームでなされる）キュレーションへ。もちろん、どちらが「よい」キュレーションかということではなく、キュレーションのあり方の拡張という意味で。

大坂 これまでは予算を増やし参加アーティストを増やし、パビリオンを増やし、サテライト会場を増やし……と拡張する流れだったけど、今回のキュレーターチームはかなりスケールを絞ってビエンナーレホールの本会場だけにしたのは、そういった流れに関係していると思います。スケールを上げて膨大なストレスを拡散して関係者が疲弊し離脱していくように状況を作らないこと。それもキュレーターやディレクターの役目だというのは、とても真っ当な感覚だと思いますし、ケアの実践でしょう。そういう意味で、ビエンナーレを運営側やオーディエンスのコミュニティのサイズに合ったスケールにしていこうというのは良い流れだと思います。

遊園地「よみうりランド」 （東京都稲城市、神奈川県川崎市）で 10月29日(木)から、17シーズン目となる「よみうりランド ジュエルミネーション2026」が始まります。今シーズンも「LIGHT is LOVE」をグランドテーマとし、人や自然、地球への愛を表現します。サブテーマには新たに「Growing Light」を掲げ、地球の宝である「緑」にフォーカスし、植物が芽生え、育ち、葉を広げていく生命力を光の演出と空間構成によって表現します。そして、「成長」「生命力」「調和」「癒し」などの宝石言葉を有するグリーン系の宝石をモチーフにした新色イルミネーションが２年ぶりに登場します。

また今シーズンは、プールWAIの人気スポット「グランド・サンクチュアリ」の中を通り抜けられるようになり、オブジェに入るという新体験とともに、これまでにない距離感での写真撮影が楽しめます。

今年度の文化勲章受章が決まった石井幹子さんがプロデュース

2010年にスタートした「よみうりランド ジュエルミネーション」は、ここでしか見ることができない宝石色のイルミネーションと東京の大夜景が一度に楽しめる、他に類をみないスポットです。今年も世界で活躍する照明デザイナー石井 幹子 氏がプロデュースします。石井氏は、2026年度の文化勲章受章が決まりました。また、イルミネーションには地球にやさしい「グリーン電力」を使用します。

ジュエルミネーションとは 石井幹子デザイン事務所が開発した世界初の宝石色をイメージしたLEDを使ったイルミネーション。ジュエリー+イルミネーションの造語です。「ジュエルミネーション」は株式会社よみうりランドの登録商標です。

今シーズンの特徴 ■新色「グローインググリーン・ジュエリーカラー」 サブテーマ「Growing Light」に合わせ、「成長」「生命力」「調和」「癒し」などの宝石言葉を持つグリーン系の宝石をモチーフにした、新色のイルミネーション「グローインググリーン・ジュエリーカラー」が登場します。入園してすぐに見渡せる広場「ジュエリー・プラザ」では、この新色イルミネーションが木々やアトラクションを彩り、植物の生命力を感じる瑞々しい空間が広がります。

■オブジェの中に入る新体験「グランド・サンクチュアリ」 プールWAIのアスレチックエリア「わいわいジャングル」が様々な愛が共存するサンクチュアリ(聖域)をイメージしたシンボルオブジェに姿を変えます。今シーズンからオブジェの中を通り抜けられるようになり、オブジェに入るという新体験とともに、これまでにない距離感での写真撮影が楽しめます。

■噴水×レーザー×炎で大迫力の「噴水ショー」 毎年大人気の噴水ショーを今年も「波のプールエリア」で開催します。高さ15ｍの巨大リングのウォータースクリーン映像や226本の噴水、レーザーと炎による演出で、圧倒的なスケールでお届けします。今年はジュエルミネーションのテーマである「Growing Light」のほか、２種類の噴水ショーが楽しめます。

■地球にやさしいグリーン電力を使用 今年も「よみうりランド ジュエルミネーション」に、風力などの自然エネルギーによって発電されたグリーン電力を使用します。グリーン電力は、発電の際にCO2を発生しないと考えられており、環境への負荷が小さいエネルギーです。ジュエルミネーションは、2010年の開始当初からLEDの使用により電力使用の抑制に努め、2021年からはグリーン電力の使用により更なる環境負荷の軽減へと取り組んでいます。

そのほかの見どころ ☆ジュエリー・グランオブジェ ジュエルミネーションのシンボルの一つである観覧車「Sky-Go-LAND」を「ジュエリー・グランオブジェ」と称してライトアップします。片側(東面)はダイヤモンドのブリリアントカットをモチーフに、14色の宝石のような輝きをジュエリーカラーで表現します。反対側(西面)は、上半分は豊かさや高貴さを感じる金色、下半分はロマンスや優しさをイメージさせるピンク色で照らしあげ、グランドテーマである「LIGHT is LOVE」を表現します。

☆ジュエリー・プロムナード 全長180mの光の並木道です。イルミネーションを樹木1本ごとに美しいグラデーションとなるように飾り付けます。今回は低木にもダイヤモンドカラーを飾り付けることで、並木道全体がさらに清楚な彩りに包まれます。

☆クリスタル・パサージュ 全長約140mの光のトンネルです。植物の蔓が伸びていくように連なる宝石の結晶モチーフが、色彩豊かなグラデーションとともに「Growing Light」の世界を鮮やかに描き出します。

☆ジュエリー・ストリーム 今年のサブテーマである「Growing Light」を表現したオブジェが、流れるプールの中央に登場します。その周囲では壮大なスケールのイルミネーションの装飾と音楽が重なり合い、プール全体が生命力あふれるスポットへと変わります。

☆ラグジュアリー・ウォール 今シーズンはグッジョバ!!エリアの壁面を「木漏れ日」をモチーフとしたデザインに一新します。幾千もの葉が生み出す木漏れ日のきらめきを、重なり合う宝石色の光で表現します。

石井幹子氏 都市照明からライトオブジェや光のパフォーマンスまでと、幅広い光の領域を開拓する照明デザイナー。日本のみならず世界の各地で活躍する照明デザインの第一人者。また光文化フォーラム代表として、国内外の光文化の継承・発展にも力を注いでいる。 主な照明作品 東京タワ-、レインボ-ブリッジ、東京ゲートブリッジ、隅田川橋梁群、横浜ベイブリッジ、ブダペスト・エリザベート橋等の橋梁照明。皇居外苑、日本武道館、銀座歌舞伎座、白川郷合掌集落、姫路城、上野東照宮等の歴史的建造物。創エネ・あかりパーク、ジャポニスム2018「エッフェル塔 日本の光を纏う」等の光イベントなど。 主な受賞 2000年に照明デザインへの貢献により、紫綬褒章を受章。2019年に文化功労者、2020年には名誉都民に選ばれ、2023年に旭日中綬章受章。国内外での受賞多数。

「よみうりランド ジュエルミネーション2026」開催に寄せて ジュエルミネーションは 2010 年の開始以来、宝石をテーマに光のデザインを追求し、独自の輝きを創出してきました。宝石と同様に、「水」や「緑」も地球が生んだ尊い宝物です。よみうりランドには広い水面が広がり、園内には桜をはじめとした豊かな緑が息づいています。今回は、この「緑」にフォーカスし、園内の多様な緑を宝石色のイルミネーションで輝かせ、木々に揺れ水面に映る光によって、これまでにない美しい効果を生み出し、新たな印象を創り出します。

To celebrate the arrival of your “Favorites”, we are offering new subscribers a special discount until November 20th. With the promo code ODLPBOOKMARK26 and this link , you will benefit from a price of €59.00 for the first year, then €79.00 per year (regular price), with no long term commitment.

The Eye of Photography is more than 45,000 articles and more than 430,000 photographs , each one carefully selected by our team before being published. Enough to make wonderful discoveries every day… and to struggle to find them again afterwards. That is exactly what ‘Favoriyes” bookmarks are here to change.

Your Favorites © The Eye of Photography

How it works

One click to keep an article

On every article and every event in our listings, a small “Add to bookmarks” icon is waiting for you. One click and it’s saved. Right away, a window offers to file it straight into a collection , an existing one or a new one you create on the spot. No time to sort? Just click elsewhere: your bookmark is safely kept, and you can file it later.

Add to your Favorites © The Eye of Photography

Collections that look like you

“To read this weekend”, “Paris shows”, “Photo books to give”… Collections carry whatever names you give them , and a single article can belong to several of them. You can rename or delete them at any time.

Find everything, wherever you are

A small black button at the bottom left of the screen opens your list from any page of the site, and the My bookmarks page shows it in full. There you can filter your bookmarks by collection, by type (articles or events) and by section. And since everything is saved to your account, you find the same list on your computer and on your phone , as soon as you are logged in.

Category – Portfolios © The Eye of Photography

Category – Saul Leiter © The Eye of Photography

Three ideas to get you started

Plan your exhibition outings: You spot an exhibition in our listings, then another, then a festival at the other end of the country? Drop them into an “Exhibitions to see” collection. The day you have a free afternoon, your programme is already waiting.

Keep your reading for later: A long interview found on a Tuesday morning, a portfolio that deserves more than a glance between two meetings: one “To read again” collection, and you come back to them in peace, on Sunday, with a coffee.

Build your own photo library

A feature for our premium subscribers

article_text:
Art Review

What Mary Lovelace O'Neal Left Behind

"Requiem" is a fitting self-elegy for the painter, precisely because nothing about it feels mournful.

Upon her death in May 2026, the abstract painter Mary Lovelace O’Neal left behind a monumental body of work. Her oeuvre includes signature large blackened canvases, marked by fluid, ecstatic gestures in neon paint that resemble the glowing afterimages of a moving flame. O’Neal’s first posthumous exhibition, Requiem, is a fitting self-elegy for the painter precisely because nothing about it feels mournful.

The work could not be more vital, and in it one feels the artist’s energetic and intuitive handling of paint as a kind of physical charge. O’Neal’s compositions transmit a powerful sense of presence and force, as though inviting viewers into the vicarious experience of an artist grappling with the formal concerns of color and line before transcending them.

The result is an almost oceanic feeling, one I imagine is equally profound in the making of a painting as staggering as the intense, cascading standout “Requiem for a Daffodil” (1997). The black, fingerlike marks that protrude from the surrounding deep navy seem to be reaching for the floral clusters and reeds in the painting’s top half, like a perpetual grasping at splendor in the shadows.

Though non-representational, these works continually approach figuration, filled with partial outlines of human and animal forms. These half-figures peer through their dark surroundings, like the pink mass in the center of “What’s Time to a Pig” (c. 1990s), and are caught in a constant state of emergence. Like an act of divine creation, O’Neal captures the transformation of raw material into something seemingly miraculous through the hands of a master craftsman.

During this formative and fruitful period between the 1970s and 1990s, when her visual language and iconoclastic artistic sensibility crystallized, O’Neal was also coming into her own as an artist. She was a groundbreaking student, becoming the first Black woman to receive an MFA from Columbia University in 1969, and in 1985, she became the first African American professor to receive tenure in UC Berkeley’s Department of Art Practice.

The back room offers a rich sketch of the painter’s life as it intersected with both world history and art history. Born in Jackson, Mississippi, in 1942, Jim Crow was fully in place in the American South during the artist’s childhood. She attended Howard University in 1960 alongside David Driskell and Lois Mailou Jones, dated the activist Stokely Carmichael, and was an activist in her own right.

The archival materials reveal the cultural and political concerns of O’Neal’s time. It’s all the more remarkable that she navigated these constraints while retaining the verve and genuine, delightful strangeness these paintings must have necessitated. “Untitled” (n.d.) gets at the humor and irreverence of O’Neal’s style. An Uncle Sam-like figure, half-covered in chalky white paint, evokes a satirical Ralph Bakshi cartoon, with many identifying features erased. It has a winking quality. Though political in nature, it foregrounds O’Neal’s formal concerns, which circle mainly around the possibilities of certain pigments (like the enveloping darkness of lampblack contrasted with punchy neons) and the permeable boundary between abstraction and figuration. It is this formal rigor that made O’Neal trailblazing in more ways than one –– both as a Black American shattering institutional barriers and as a woman painter making important interventions into the inherited, lionized artistic movements of the Color Field, Abstract Expressionism, and Minimalism.

Mary Lovelace O'Neal, "Race Woman Series #7" (1992-93), mixed media on canvas (left); Mary Lovelace O'Neal, "Untitled" (n.d.), mixed media and oil on canvas

“Race Woman Series #7” (1992–93) dramatizes the tension between the structural or compositional and the political, suggesting that it was an enduring preoccupation for the artist. A dazed face vaguely springs up from a prominent green being, which could just be read as an indecipherable scrawl, while a white specter at the top of the canvas drips over it. O’Neal’s use of color is frenetic and instinctive, resulting in a painting that is too varied to slot into a clear interpretation. Like the Klannish chiaroscuro of Norman Lewis’ “ Alabama ” (1960), the legibility of “Race Woman Series #7” relies on the light its instructive title sheds on it.

But unlike Lewis, when we search for correlation between O’Neal’s caption and the canvas, we are pulled deeper into her self-reflexive, numinous and unrepeatable idiom, which makes its own intuitive sense and, anyway, seeks to go beyond sense-making into the terrain of near-mystical experience.

Mary Lovelace O’Neal: Requiem continues at Boesky Gallery (509 West 24th Street, Chelsea, Manhattan) through December 19. The exhibition is organized by the gallery.

article_text:
Universal’s horror entry “ Other Mommy ,” directed by Rob Savage and starring Jessica Chastain and Jay Duplass, squeaked to the top of the U.K. and Ireland box office in a dead heat, debuting at No. 1 with £1.97 million ($2.66 million).

The horror debut narrowly edged Sony’s psychological thriller “ Verity ,” which moved to second place in its sophomore session by a razor-thin margin of just £33,263 ($43,970), collecting £1.94 million ($2.62 million). The Colleen Hoover adaptation lifted its running cume to £7.3 million ($9.8 million).

Jeremy Clarkson Returns to Automobiles in New ‘Clarkson’s Farm’ Special ‘Jeremy Grows a Car’

Paramount’s action thriller “Heart of the Beast,” starring Brad Pitt and J.K. Simmons, held third position in its third frame with $1.1 million, elevating its gross to $7.3 million. Sony’s franchise reboot “Resident Evil” took fourth spot in its fourth session, generating $1 million to advance its total to $17.1 million. Sony also claimed fifth position with the debut of Aaron Sorkin’s political drama “The Social Reckoning,” which collected $840,538.

Universal’s “Sense and Sensibility” followed in sixth place during its third weekend, adding $797,038 for a running total of $6.8 million. Entertainment Film Distributors’ historical drama “The Uprising,” directed by Paul Greengrass and starring Andrew Garfield, opened in seventh position with $732,547.

Studiocanal’s animated feature “Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom” landed in eighth place in its fourth session, collecting $665,849 to raise its total to $5.1 million. Warner Bros.’ Tom Cruise film “Digger” took ninth position in its sophomore frame, taking $661,819 to bring its cume to $3 million. Universal’s “ The Odyssey ,” directed by Christopher Nolan, rounded out the top 10 in its 13th week on release, adding $353,321 to push its cumulative gross to $118.3 million.

Looking ahead to the upcoming theatrical frame, Monday saw Trafalgar Releasing launching music documentary “Always Lalisa,” followed on Tuesday by Cinematik presenting “ENB: The Sleeping Beauty” across 100+ locations.

Wide commercial and saturation rollouts on Friday opening across 300+ locations are led by Disney’s survival thriller “Whalefall,” directed by Brian Duffield and starring Austin Abrams and Josh Brolin; Icon Film Distribution’s found-footage horror “The Influencer Project,” starring Chiara King; and Trafalgar Releasing’s filmed stage capture of “Hadestown: The Musical,” starring Reeve Carney and Eva Noblezada. Paramount is also rolling out “Street Fighter”.

Mid-tier and platform releases across 100+ locations include Universal’s animated feature “Forgotten Island,” directed by Joel Crawford and Januel P. Mercado, and Anime Ltd.’s anime re-release “Arrietty,” featuring voice work from Saoirse Ronan and Tom Holland.

Specialized, festival, and international titles arriving Friday include Conic’s drama “Case 137,” directed by Dominik Moll, across 25+ screens; Soilsiu Films’ documentary “Forever Is Now,” directed by Neasa Ní Chianáin, across 25+ sites; DOVC U.K.’s “Deadline,” directed by Kiwi Chow across 25+ screens; Central City Media’s “It’s My Time,” directed by Xue Bai and starring Michelle Yeoh across 25+ locations; Bulldog Film Distribution’s “By Design,” directed by Amanda Kramer and starring Juliette Lewis; Signature Entertainment’s “Winter of the Crow”; Exposure’s “Mistura”; Dogwoof’s “Naza”; and Bakrania Media’s “Prahaar.”

Repertory and archival screenings are highlighted by Hammer and Icon Film Distribution launching Terence Fisher’s classic “Dracula” in a 4K restoration across 100+ screens, alongside Park Circus’ 25th anniversary 4K restoration of Alejandro Amenábar’s “The Others,” starring Nicole Kidman, across 100+ locations. The frame concludes on Saturday with Trafalgar Releasing’s live event cinema broadcast of the Metropolitan Opera’s “Macbeth”.

Are Black Cats Modernity’s Icons?

How Manet transformed the misunderstood feline into an emblem of independent thinking; plus, Gay Halloween memes galore!

Centuries of superstition may be to blame for black cats facing among the lowest adoption outcomes at shelters across the US. But these mysterious, furry angels have shed at least part of their witchy stereotype in the modern era — thanks largely to 19th-century French artists, argues Rebecca Rebecca Schiffman, Hyperallergic associate editor. According to Schiffman, who makes a case for the black cat as a modern icon in art history in an essay perfectly timed for Hallows' Eve, painters such as Édouard Manet helped dark-furred felines come to symbolize a Belle Époque “appetite for provocation” and “refusal to be domesticated.”

On a related note, a big, heartfelt thanks to all who joined us at Hyperallergic ’s Halloween party last night — you blew us all away with your commitment to the art costumes. (I’m looking at you, “Two Fridas” and “Saturn Devouring His Son.”) Look out for photos from the evening soon!

And in another tradition, Staff Writer Rhea Nayyar rounds up the spiciest Gay Halloween memes this year, a trend that holds a mirror up to our broader pop-culture moment. “ I hate gay Halloween, what do you mean we're dressed as Kelly Clarkson and an animatronic bird?”

—Valentina Di Liscia, senior editor

How Édouard Manet’s Black Cat Became a Symbol of Modernity

Every Halloween, black cats return as emblems of witchcraft, bad luck, and the supernatural. Their sinister reputations stretch back centuries: starting in the Middle Ages, people associated cats with heresy and sexual transgression, and their perceived affinity with witches intensified during the trials of Elizabeth Francis and Agnes Waterhouse and their cat Sathan between 1565-1579.

But after the Enlightenment, 19th-century French artists and writers began to reclaim the mysterious and devilish qualities foisted onto felines as desirable.| Rebecca Schiffman
